prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I shall never get you put together entirely, Pieced, glued, and properly jointed. Mule-bray, pig-grunt and bawdy cackles Proceed from your great lips. It’s worse than a barnyard. Perhaps you consider yourself an oracle, Mouthpiece of the dead, or of some god or other. Thirty years now I have labored To dredge the silt from your throat. I am none the wiser. Scaling little ladders with glue pots and pails of lysol I crawl like an ant in mourning Over the weedy acres of your brow To mend the immense skull plates and clear The bald, white tumuli of your eyes. A blue sky out of the Oresteia Arches above us. O father, all by yourself You are pithy and historical as the Roman Forum. I open my lunch on a hill of black cypress. Your fluted bones and acanthine hair are littered In their old anarchy to the horizon-line. It would take more than a lightning-stroke To create such a ruin. Nights, I squat in the cornucopia Of your left ear, out of the wind, Counting the red stars and those of plum-color. The sun rises under the pillar of your tongue. My hours are married to shadow. No longer do I listen for the scrape of a keel On the blank stones of the landing.

outputs.L1:
I shall never reassemble you entirely—  
pieced, glued, and properly jointed.  
Mule-brays, pig-grunts, and bawdy cackles  
issue from your great lips.  
It is worse than a barnyard.

Perhaps you consider yourself an oracle,  
a mouthpiece of the dead,  
or of some god or other.  
For thirty years now, I have labored  
to dredge the silt from your throat.  
I am none the wiser.

Scaling little ladders with glue pots  
and pails of Lysol,  
I crawl like an ant in mourning  
over the weedy acres of your brow,  
to mend the immense plates of your skull  
and clear the bald, white tumuli of your eyes.

A blue sky from the *Oresteia*  
arches above us.  
O father, all by yourself,  
you are as pithy and historical  
as the Roman Forum.

I open my lunch  
on a hill of black cypress.  
Your fluted bones and acanthine hair  
lie scattered in their old anarchy  
to the horizon line.  
It would take more than a lightning stroke  
to create such a ruin.

At night, I squat in the cornucopia  
of your left ear, sheltered from the wind,  
counting the red stars  
and those of plum color.  
The sun rises beneath  
the pillar of your tongue.  
My hours are wedded to shadow.

No longer do I listen  
for the scrape of a keel  
on the blank stones of the landing.

The speaker describes a long and futile effort to piece together a vast, broken figure. This figure is not merely damaged; it is monumental, fragmented, and almost impossible to comprehend. The speaker has tried to reconstruct it, to make sense of its scattered parts, but every attempt fails. The task seems too large for any single person, and the figure remains incomplete and resistant to understanding.

The figure itself is presented in unsettling terms. It is noisy, grotesque, and strangely powerful, producing sounds that are difficult to interpret. At times, it seems almost sacred, as though it might once have been revered as an oracle or a divine mouthpiece. Yet instead of offering clear wisdom, it gives only confusion, distortion, and unintelligible noise. Its authority is therefore both impressive and hollow: it appears grand and meaningful, but it does not provide the enlightenment the speaker seeks.

The speaker has devoted thirty years to this effort, trying to “clear” the figure’s throat and understand what it might be saying. This suggests a long history of emotional, intellectual, or spiritual labor. The speaker has hoped that if the figure could be repaired or made to speak clearly, it might finally reveal some truth. However, despite decades of attention and devotion, the speaker remains unenlightened. The figure’s message, if it has one, remains inaccessible.

The figure’s body is imagined as an immense ruin spread across a mythic landscape. Its parts are so enormous that they seem to belong not to an ordinary human body, but to a fallen giant or ancient statue. This imagery gives the figure a legendary scale, connecting it to ideas of lost civilizations, broken monuments, and ruined gods. The speaker moves among these remains as though living inside the wreckage of something once powerful but now collapsed.

By the end, the speaker appears resigned to this condition. Rather than expecting the figure to be restored, or waiting for some outside force to bring rescue or revelation, the speaker accepts life in its shadow. The broken figure continues to dominate the speaker’s world, but the hope of arrival, rescue, or final understanding has faded. What remains is endurance: the speaker lives among the ruins, shaped by the presence of the figure but no longer expecting it to speak clearly or be made whole.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a speaker who is consumed by the impossible task of reconstructing a ruined father figure. The father is imagined as a vast, broken monument, like a fallen statue from the ancient world, whose fragments are scattered and difficult to interpret. Through images of repair, excavation, and archaeology, the speaker tries to piece him back together and recover some meaning from what remains. This labor suggests not only physical restoration but also an emotional and psychological attempt to understand a lost parent.

However, the task proves futile. The speaker has spent years working among the ruins, scraping, cleaning, and listening for signs of wisdom, but the father remains silent and incomplete. His immense scale makes him overwhelming, while his brokenness makes him unknowable. The imagery of myth and antiquity emphasizes both his power and his distance: he is larger than life, yet also lifeless, fragmented, and inaccessible.

As a result, the poem becomes less about successful reconstruction than about the persistence of grief. The speaker’s devotion does not lead to healing or clarity. Instead, it reveals how paternal absence continues to dominate her life. The dead father cannot be restored, and the daughter cannot become whole by trying to rebuild him. The poem therefore portrays mourning as an endless, exhausting process, shaped by love, resentment, reverence, and frustration. In the end, the ruined father remains a monument to loss, and the speaker remains trapped in the shadow of what can never be fully recovered.

Pieced together from old maps, dusty letters, and stories told by travelers, the legend of the Mule Trail remained a mystery for generations. It was said that a stubborn mule once carried a hidden message across the mountains during a terrible storm, refusing to stop even when the path disappeared beneath snow and stone.

Many tried to follow the same route, but few knew how to proceed. The trail was broken, the landmarks were faded, and the truth seemed buried in time. Still, each clue brought the explorers closer to understanding the journey. In the end, they discovered that the real treasure was not gold or jewels, but the courage to continue when the way forward was uncertain.

counterfactuals.output:
I can write an original poem with a confessional, modernist intensity and imagery of repairing a colossal ruined father figure.

**Repair**

I bring the ladder,  
the little surgical tin,  
the spool of wire bright as a nerve.

All morning I climb you—  
knee, rib, blackened lapel—  
a continent of soot and old weather.

Father, your mouth is a fallen arch.  
Birds have nested in the O.  
Rain keeps entering where the orders came out.

I have my needle.  
I have my dutiful thread.  
I stitch the crack in your cheek  
and the crack widens, smiling.

Below, the town lifts its pale faces.  
They want you standing again,  
buttoned, bronze,  
your shadow laid neatly over the square.

But inside your chest  
there is no engine,  
only rooms full of ash,  
chairs turned toward a wall.

I crawl in with a lamp.  
My breath comes back to me  
wearing your voice.

Daughter, daughter—  
the echo rehearses me  
until I am small enough to fit  
in the hollow of your boot.

I polish your medals.  
They bleed rust.  
I mend your hands.  
They close on air.

At dusk the moon  
hangs like a white bandage  
over your broken head.

I could spend my life here,  
patching the giant,  
feeding him nails,  
singing into the vacancy.

But the scaffold shakes.  
The seams undo themselves.  
Your great face drops  
one stone eyelid at a time.

And I, at last,  
come down carrying nothing—  
not the hammer,  
not the name,

only my own two hands,  
raw, unblessed,  
opening in the dark.
